title: Erdős Problem #578: Hypercubes in Random Graphs
description: If G is a random graph on 2^d vertices with edge probability 1/2, does G almost surely contain Q_d? Answer: YES (Riordan 2000). Threshold p > 1/4 suffices, and copies are normally distributed.

meta.author: Riordan (2000)
prerequisites: Second moment method in probabilistic combinatorics
originalContributions: Hypercube: structure with vertices = 2^d, edges = d·2^{d-1}
RandomGraph: G(n,p) model with probability constraints
erdos_578_summary: proved conjunction of main results

overview.historicalContext: Erdős and Bollobás conjectured that random graphs G(2^d, 1/2) almost surely contain the d-dimensional hypercube Q_d. This was part of a broader program studying what subgraphs appear in random graphs. Riordan (2000) solved this affirmatively, showing even p > 1/4 suffices, and proved the number of copies is normally distributed. The Erdős-Rényi random graph model G(n,p) was introduced in 1959-1960, and determining threshold probabilities for spanning subgraph containment became a central theme. Hypercubes are especially challenging because Q_d has 2^d vertices (matching the random graph size), making this a spanning subgraph problem rather than a fixed-size subgraph problem; earlier work by Bollobás and Frieze in the 1980s studied similar spanning structure questions.
overview.problemStatement:
**Problem Statement (SOLVED: YES)**

The d-dimensional hypercube Q_d has 2^d vertices and d·2^{d-1} edges.

**Question:** If G is a random graph on 2^d vertices with edge probability p = 1/2, does G almost surely contain a copy of Q_d?

**Answer:** YES (Riordan 2000)

**Strengthening:** Even p > 1/4 suffices (Riordan 2000)
overview.proofStrategy: The formalization defines the hypercube Q_d, random graph model G(n,p), and 'almost surely' containment. Riordan's theorem is axiomatized for p > 1/4, from which the original p = 1/2 conjecture follows. The threshold optimality at 1/4 and normal distribution of copies are also axiomatized. The summary theorem proves the conjunction of the conjecture and threshold result.
keyInsights: **Spanning vs fixed-size:** Unlike most random graph containment problems where the subgraph has fixed size, $Q_d$ has $2^d$ vertices — matching the random graph — making this a spanning subgraph problem, which is inherently harder

**Threshold surprise:** The threshold $p_0 = 1/4$ is unexpectedly low — intuitively, containing a structured spanning subgraph in a random graph should require high density, yet only 25% edge probability suffices

**Second moment power:** Riordan's proof demonstrates the second moment method at its most powerful: bounding $\mathbb{E}[X^2]/(\mathbb{E}[X])^2 \to 1$ requires careful counting of overlapping hypercube copies, the combinatorial heart of the argument

**Measure-free formalization:** The Lean formalization sidesteps measure theory entirely by encoding 'almost surely' as a deterministic $\forall \varepsilon > 0, \exists D, \forall d \geq D$ statement — capturing the asymptotic behavior without needing Mathlib's probability measure infrastructure

**From existence to distribution:** Riordan proved not just that copies exist but that their count is normally distributed — a much stronger result showing copies behave like approximately independent events

sections.title: Part I: Hypercube Definitions
sections.summary: Hypercube structure with vertices = 2^d, edges = d·2^{d-1}. Helper functions hypercubeVertexCount and hypercubeEdgeCount. Verified by examples for d=3.
sections.mathContext: $|V(Q_d)| = 2^d$, $|E(Q_d)| = d \cdot 2^{d-1}$ since each vertex has degree $d$ and each edge is counted twice.

sections.title: Part II: Random Graph Model
sections.summary: RandomGraph structure with n vertices and edge probability p ∈ [0,1]. Two constructors: standardRandomGraph (p=1/2) and riordanRandomGraph (p>1/4).
sections.mathContext: The Erdős-Rényi model $G(n,p)$: each of $\binom{n}{2}$ edges appears independently with probability $p$. For $n = 2^d$, $p = 1/2$: expected $\sim 2^{2d-1}$ edges, far exceeding $Q_d$'s $d \cdot 2^{d-1}$.

sections.title: Parts III-IV: Almost Sure Containment and Conjecture
sections.summary: AlmostSurely: ∀ ε>0, ∃ D, ∀ d≥D, P(d). ContainsHypercube: abstract subgraph containment. erdos_bollobas_conjecture: the original problem statement.
sections.mathContext: Captures $\Pr[Q_d \subseteq G(2^d, p)] \to 1$ as $d \to \infty$ without measure theory.

sections.title: Part V: Riordan's Theorem (2000)
sections.summary: Two axioms: riordan_theorem (p>1/4 suffices) and erdos_bollobas_proved (original conjecture). Riordan's result is strictly stronger.
sections.mathContext: The key axiom: $\forall p > 1/4,\; G(2^d, p) \supseteq Q_d$ almost surely. Since $1/2 > 1/4$, the original conjecture follows.

sections.title: Part VI: Threshold and Distribution
sections.summary: Two axioms: threshold_at_quarter (p₀=1/4 is optimal) and copies_normally_distributed (count of Q_d copies is asymptotically normal).
sections.mathContext: Phase transition at $p_0 = 1/4$: $\Pr[Q_d \subseteq G] \to 1$ for $p > 1/4$, $\to 0$ for $p < 1/4$. The CLT result strengthens existence to distributional information.

sections.title: Part VII: Hypercube Properties
sections.summary: Regularity: degree d (proved by rfl). Automorphisms: |Aut(Q_d)| = d!·2^d (hyperoctahedral group). Verified for d=3.
sections.mathContext: $\text{Aut}(Q_d) \cong B_d = S_d \ltimes (\mathbb{Z}/2)^d$ with $|B_d| = d! \cdot 2^d$. This symmetry group governs the expected copy count.

sections.title: Part VIII: Summary Theorem
sections.summary: erdos_578_summary: proves the conjunction of erdos_bollobas_conjecture ∧ threshold_at_quarter via And.intro of two axioms.
sections.mathContext: The summary theorem $\text{erdos\_578\_summary} := \langle \text{erdos\_bollobas\_proved},\; \text{threshold\_at\_quarter} \rangle$ packages both results.

conclusion.summary: Erdős Problem #578 is SOLVED with answer YES. Random graphs G(2^d, 1/2) almost surely contain the hypercube Q_d. Riordan strengthened this to any p > 1/4 and showed the number of copies is normally distributed. The threshold 1/4 is essentially optimal.
conclusion.implications: This result is a landmark in the study of spanning subgraph thresholds in random graphs. It demonstrates that even highly structured spanning subgraphs (hypercubes) appear at surprisingly low edge densities. The second moment method, pushed to its limits here, became a template for subsequent threshold results. The normal distribution of copies connects to the general theory of subgraph counts in random graphs, with implications for property testing and average-case complexity of subgraph isomorphism.
openQuestions: What is the exact threshold probability for hypercube containment?
What are the precise constants in the normal distribution?
How does this generalize to other structured subgraphs?
